intro: In this college you'll learn how to make plans in Dutch: invite a friend, accept or politely say no, ask a colleague to cover your shift, talk about your days off, and use simple future and modal verbs.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — talking about plans
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme eleven. Its title is a question you will use all the time: [[Wat gaan we doen?]], which means 'What are we going to do?'. This whole theme is about making plans with other people. You will learn to invite someone, to say a happy 'yes', to say a polite 'no', and to arrange things with friends and with colleagues at work. A few useful words first. A plan is [[een plan]]. An appointment or arrangement is [[een afspraak]], and this word is everywhere in Dutch life. An invitation is [[een uitnodiging]]. Your free time is [[vrije tijd]], and a day off work is [[een vrije dag]]. The Dutch love to plan ahead, so you will hear these words constantly. As always, I explain everything in clear English, but every Dutch word and sentence you hear is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so your ear and your pronunciation grow at the same time. Please repeat each Dutch phrase out loud after me — that is how it sticks. There is also a lovely Dutch word for a cosy, pleasant get-together: [[gezellig]]. You cannot really translate it, but you will feel it the moment friends gather. So, are you ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]] Let's begin.

paragraphs.heading: The future with gaan
paragraphs.text: The easiest way to talk about the future in Dutch is with the verb [[gaan]], which means 'to go', plus another verb. It works just like English 'going to'. You put [[gaan]] in the right form, and the main verb waits at the very end of the sentence. So 'I am going to cook tonight' is [[Ik ga vanavond koken.]] Notice [[koken]], 'to cook', sits right at the end. The forms are easy: 'I go' is [[ik ga]], 'you go' is [[jij gaat]], and 'we go' is [[wij gaan]]. So our theme question, 'What are we going to do this weekend?', is [[Wat gaan we dit weekend doen?]] To answer, you might say [[We gaan zaterdag naar de markt.]], 'We are going to the market on Saturday'. Or, for a quiet evening, [[Ik ga vanavond een film kijken.]], 'I am going to watch a film tonight'. Here is a small secret: for a fixed plan with a clear time, Dutch people often just use the present tense. So 'Tomorrow I am not working' is simply [[Morgen werk ik niet.]] Both ways are completely normal. Try making your own plan now, out loud: take [[Ik ga]], add a time like [[morgen]], and finish with an activity. [[Heel goed!]]

paragraphs.heading: Inviting: shall we, do you feel like?
paragraphs.text: Now let's invite someone. The friendliest way to suggest doing something together starts with the words [[Zullen we]], which mean 'Shall we'. Again, the main verb goes to the end of the question. So 'Shall we eat together tonight?' is [[Zullen we vanavond samen eten?]], and 'Shall we arrange to meet at three o'clock?' is [[Zullen we om drie uur afspreken?]] That verb [[afspreken]] means 'to arrange to meet', and it is one of the most Dutch words there is. A second very natural invitation is [[Ga je mee?]], which means 'Are you coming along?'. You will hear it everywhere: [[Wij gaan naar de bioscoop, ga je mee?]], 'We're going to the cinema, are you coming?'. A softer, warmer version asks about your feelings: [[Heb je zin om mee te gaan?]], 'Do you feel like coming along?'. That phrase [[zin hebben]] means 'to feel like' doing something, and it sounds friendly and open. If it is a party, you might say [[Ik nodig je uit voor mijn feest.]], 'I invite you to my party'. And to set the details, you ask [[Hoe laat en waar spreken we af?]], 'What time and where shall we meet?'. Practise inviting a friend now: start with [[Zullen we]] and add your own activity at the end.

paragraphs.heading: Saying yes — and saying no kindly
paragraphs.text: When you get an invitation, you need a warm 'yes' and a kind 'no'. To accept, the simplest happy answers are [[Ja, leuk!]], 'Yes, nice!', and [[Dat is een goed idee!]], 'That's a good idea!'. You can add a question to fix the plan: [[Ja, leuk! Hoe laat spreken we af?]], 'Yes, nice! What time shall we meet?'. Now, saying 'no' is an art, and the golden rule is simple: a polite Dutch 'no' almost always comes with a short reason. Do not just say [[nee]] on its own — it sounds cold. Instead, start softly with [[Sorry]] and give a reason using the little word [[want]], which means 'because'. For example: [[Sorry, dat komt niet uit, want ik moet werken.]], 'Sorry, that doesn't suit me, because I have to work'. That phrase [[dat komt niet uit]] is the perfect polite way to say something doesn't fit your schedule. You can also say [[Ik kan helaas niet komen.]], 'Unfortunately I can't come', where [[helaas]] means 'unfortunately'. And always leave the door open with [[Misschien een andere keer?]], 'Maybe another time?'. With a friendly reason, your 'no' stays warm and your friendship stays strong.

paragraphs.heading: Modal verbs and asking a colleague
paragraphs.text: To talk about plans and work, you need three little helper verbs called modals. The first is [[willen]], 'to want': [[Ik wil graag komen.]] means 'I would like to come'. The second is [[kunnen]], 'to be able to, can': [[Ik kan vandaag niet.]] means 'I can't today'. The third is [[mogen]], 'to be allowed to, may': [[Mag ik vrijdag vrij?]] means 'May I have Friday off?'. With each modal, the main verb again goes to the end. These are perfect at work. Imagine you cannot do your shift, your [[dienst]]. You can ask a colleague, [[een collega]], to cover for you with [[Kun je voor mij invallen?]], 'Can you cover for me?'. The verb [[invallen]] means 'to stand in' for someone. Or you suggest a swap: [[Zullen we van dienst ruilen?]], 'Shall we swap shifts?'. To ask your manager for a day off politely, use the [[u]] form: [[Kan ik vrijdag een vrije dag krijgen?]], 'Can I get Friday off?'. And remember the days of the week, because you need them: [[maandag, dinsdag, woensdag, donderdag, vrijdag, zaterdag, zondag]]. There is even a Dutch saying about keeping your word: [[Afspraak is afspraak.]], 'A deal is a deal'.

paragraphs.heading: Making plans with a friend
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together the way it really happens. Imagine your friend Nadia messages you. She asks [[Hoi! Wat ga jij dit weekend doen?]], 'Hi! What are you going to do this weekend?'. You don't have plans yet, so you reply [[Nog niets. Heb jij een idee?]], 'Nothing yet. Do you have an idea?'. She suggests [[Zaterdag is mijn verjaardag. Zullen we samen eten?]], 'Saturday is my birthday. Shall we eat together?'. But you work on Saturday, so you say kindly [[Leuk! Maar zaterdag moet ik werken. Dat komt niet uit.]] Then you offer a solution with a modal verb: [[Ik ga een collega vragen of hij kan invallen.]], 'I'm going to ask a colleague whether he can cover'. Nadia is delighted and says [[Top! We spreken om zeven uur af bij het restaurant.]], 'Great! Let's meet at seven o'clock at the restaurant'. See how naturally [[gaan]], [[zullen we]] and the modals all work together? Now it is your turn. Today, send one real Dutch message to a friend or colleague: invite them, or politely arrange something. There is a lovely Dutch proverb for this: [[Hoe meer zielen, hoe meer vreugd.]], 'The more souls, the more joy' — the more the merrier. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done, and I'll see you in theme twelve!
